When a Correct Reward Is Not Enough: Diagnosing and Guiding PPO in an Analytically Solved Broker–Trader Game

Conference: ACM International Conference on AI in Finance; November 14–17, 2026; Milan, ItalyCCS: Computing methodologies Reinforcement learningCCS: Applied computing Economics
Siu Tung Wong Affiliation: Institute of Finance and Technology, University College London, Gower Street, London, WC1E 6BT, United Kingdom email: ucesstw@ucl.ac.uk and Carlo Campajola Affiliation: Institute of Finance and Technology, University College London, Gower Street, London, WC1E 6BT, United Kingdom Affiliation: UZH Blockchain Center, Andreasstrasse 15, Zürich, 8050, Switzerland email: c.campajola@ucl.ac.uk
© , 2026
Abstract.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used for financial optimal-control problems when complex dynamics make analytical strategies difficult to obtain. There are financial mathematics literactures which provides many solved models whose equations and controls could evaluate and guide learning; we ask whether RL can exploit these results.

We place a proximal policy optimisation (PPO) agent in an analytically solved continuous-time broker–trader game. PPO replaces the broker and chooses its trading speed while interacting with an informed trader and stochastic uninformed order flow. We derive a finite-step reward from the broker’s continuous-time payoff and verify its discrete implementation through grid refinement and an exact one-step identity. With zero uninformed flow, a validation-selected PPO–FFNN approaches the reference action. With stochastic uninformed flow, the tested PPO–FFNN and PPO–LSTM remain inaccurate, although supervised learning confirms that their actors can represent the action. Monte Carlo diagnostics show that their critics do not reliably rank nearby actions; potential-based reward shaping also gives no reliable improvement. Under partial information, a causal certainty-equivalent controller based on the broker’s observable history remains close to the reference, while PPO has larger errors and lower payoffs.

Finally, we freeze the analytical policy and train PPO to adjust it after the execution cost changes. Halving the cost yields a repeatable improvement that closes 2.22%2.22\% of the gap to the changed-cost reference. The analytical solution therefore provides both a benchmark for diagnosing RL and a useful starting policy for adaptation.

Keywords: 
optimal execution, stochastic control, proximal policy optimization, partial observability, potential-based reward shaping, residual reinforcement learning, model misspecification, analytical policy initialization, analytical benchmarks

1. Introduction

Optimal execution balances execution costs against inventory exposure and adverse price movements. Reinforcement learning (RL) is attractive when richer market dynamics make analytical strategies difficult to obtain. We ask whether RL can recover an analytically known broker strategy from its performance criterion and use that strategy after the environment changes.

Our environment follows the continuous-time game of Cartea, Jaimungal, and Sánchez-Betancourt (Cartea et al., 2026), who model the interaction between a broker, an informed trader, and an uninformed trader. The broker internalises client orders and hedges in the lit market. Informed flow contains private information, while rapid trading is costly and slow trading leaves inventory exposed. Their analytical equilibrium gives an action at every state, allowing same-state action comparisons together with realised payoffs and inventory trajectories.

Prior studies use RL to adjust an Almgren–Chriss schedule, learn liquidation policies against analytical benchmarks, or structure actor–critic learning with closed-form policy and value functions (Hendricks and Wilcox, 2014; Macrì and Lillo, 2024; Wang et al., 2026). They do not test whether a finite-step reward recovers the known state-dependent strategy in this broker–trader game. Analytical-policy initialisation and adaptation have also been proposed (Ning et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026). We separate discretisation, policy learning, and hidden-state estimation.

We study three research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: Full-information control. Can PPO–FFNN and PPO–LSTM recover the broker’s analytical trading strategy when every relevant state variable is observed?

  • •

    RQ2: Partial-information control. How closely can PPO–FFNN and PPO–LSTM approach the certainty-equivalent benchmark (Mania et al., 2019) when the informed trader’s inventory, signal, and current trading rate are hidden?

  • •

    RQ3: Adapting an analytical policy. When the execution cost differs from the value used to calculate the analytical policy, can PPO learn an adjustment that improves the unchanged policy?

Section 2 reviews related work, Section 3 introduces the environment, Section 4 answers RQ1–RQ2, and Section 5 answers RQ3.

2. Related Work

Analytical execution and broker games:

Analytical execution models relate trading actions to inventory, impact, order flow, and predictive signals (Cartea and Jaimungal, 2016; Casgrain and Jaimungal, 2019). Broker–trader games add strategic interaction because hedging affects prices while client orders change the broker’s inventory and information (Cartea et al., 2026; Wu and Jaimungal, 2024). We use the known broker action as the RL target.

RL for optimal execution:

RL has learned liquidation schedules through value-based methods, PPO, and continuous-time actor–critic (Nevmyvaka et al., 2006; Lin and Beling, 2020; Ning et al., 2021; Moallemi and Wang, 2022; Koulouris and Campajola, 2026). Hybrid methods adjust or initialise from an analytical schedule, or embed closed-form structure (Hendricks and Wilcox, 2014; Ning et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026). The broker–trader equilibrium instead permits same-state action comparisons. Although policy gradients have convergence results for linear–quadratic control (Fazel et al., 2018), PPO remains sensitive to implementation and evaluation choices (Engstrom et al., 2020; Andrychowicz et al., 2020; Henderson et al., 2018).

Analytical guidance and reward shaping:

Analytical equations can guide learning and provide a benchmark. Prior work adds a Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman loss or closed-form policy and value structure (Mukherjee and Liu, 2023; Wang et al., 2026). Residual RL adds a learned action to an existing controller (Johannink et al., 2019); in Section 5, we use it to adjust the frozen broker action after the execution cost changes. We also test potential-based shaping, which preserves policy ordering (Ng et al., 1999; Sowerby et al., 2022).

RL under partial information:

With hidden state, an agent can summarise observations recurrently or estimate the hidden variables explicitly (Igl et al., 2018; Lambrechts et al., 2022). We compare feedforward and recurrent PPO with a certainty-equivalent controller that updates such an estimate from observable history.

3. Environment Design

3.1. Broker Execution Game

Our baseline is the continuous-time broker–trader model of Cartea, Jaimungal, and Sánchez-Betancourt (Cartea et al., 2026). An informed trader sends orders to the broker at rate ηt\eta_{t}, uninformed clients generate flow ξt\xi_{t}, and the broker hedges the resulting inventory in a lit market at rate νt\nu_{t}. The informed trader responds to a predictive signal process α=(αt)t∈[0,T]\alpha=(\alpha_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}. PPO chooses the broker’s trading rate νt\nu_{t}, while the informed trader follows its analytical feedback rule and the uninformed flow remains exogenous.

Let QtBQ_{t}^{B} and QtIQ_{t}^{I} denote broker and informed-trader inventories, YtY_{t} the price-impact state, and StS_{t} the midprice. Their dynamics are

(1) d​ξt\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\xi_{t} =−κξ​ξt​d​t+σξ​d​Wtξ,\displaystyle=-\kappa_{\xi}\xi_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{\xi}\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{\xi}, d​St\displaystyle\mathrm{d}S_{t} =(αt+h​νt−p​Yt)​d​t+σS​d​WtS.\displaystyle=(\alpha_{t}+h\nu_{t}-pY_{t})\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{S}\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{S}.

The broker’s trade changes inventory, incurs execution cost, and affects the price at which its remaining inventory is valued.

The analytical solution gives the feedback controls

(3) ηt⋆\displaystyle\eta_{t}^{\star} =P21​(t)​QtB+P22​(t)​QtI+P23​(t)​Yt+h1​(t)​αt+h2​(t)​ξt.\displaystyle=P_{21}(t)Q^{B}_{t}+P_{22}(t)Q^{I}_{t}+P_{23}(t)Y_{t}+h_{1}(t)\alpha_{t}+h_{2}(t)\xi_{t}.

Therefore even if the PPO agent takes suboptimal-actions, the informed trader continues to use the analytical feedback rule and does not operate in subgame nash equilibrium. We refer to it as the analytical-feedback trader.

3.2. Discrete PPO Environment

We divide [0,T][0,T] into N=T/Δ​tN=T/\Delta t intervals and use left-endpoint Euler–Maruyama transitions (Higham, 2001). Define uk=νk−ηk−ξku_{k}=\nu_{k}-\eta_{k}-\xi_{k}, μk=αk+h​νk−p​Yk\mu_{k}=\alpha_{k}+h\nu_{k}-pY_{k}, ρα=1−κα​Δ​t\rho_{\alpha}=1-\kappa_{\alpha}\Delta t, and ρξ=1−κξ​Δ​t\rho_{\xi}=1-\kappa_{\xi}\Delta t. The finite-grid dynamics are

Qk+1B\displaystyle Q_{k+1}^{B} =QkB+uk​Δ​t,\displaystyle=Q_{k}^{B}+u_{k}\Delta t, Qk+1I\displaystyle Q_{k+1}^{I} =QkI+ηk​Δ​t,\displaystyle=Q_{k}^{I}+\eta_{k}\Delta t,
(6) Yk+1\displaystyle Y_{k+1} =Yk+(h​νk−p​Yk)​Δ​t,\displaystyle=Y_{k}+(h\nu_{k}-pY_{k})\Delta t, αk+1\displaystyle\alpha_{k+1} =ρα​αk+σα​Δ​Wkα\displaystyle=\rho_{\alpha}\alpha_{k}+\sigma_{\alpha}\Delta W_{k}^{\alpha}
ξk+1\displaystyle\xi_{k+1} =ρξ​ξk+σξ​Δ​Wkξ,\displaystyle=\rho_{\xi}\xi_{k}+\sigma_{\xi}\Delta W_{k}^{\xi}, Sk+1\displaystyle S_{k+1} =Sk+μk​Δ​t+σS​Δ​WkS,.\displaystyle=S_{k}+\mu_{k}\Delta t+\sigma_{S}\Delta W_{k}^{S},.

The three Δ​W\Delta W terms are independent Gaussian increments with variance Δ​t\Delta t. We define τk=(T−tk)/T\tau_{k}=(T-t_{k})/T as the fraction of the trading horizon remaining. Full-information PPO receives SkS_{k}, QkBQ_{k}^{B}, QkIQ_{k}^{I}, YkY_{k}, αk\alpha_{k}, ξk\xi_{k}, and τk\tau_{k}. Partial-information PPO receives SkS_{k}, QkBQ_{k}^{B}, YkY_{k}, ξk\xi_{k}, τk\tau_{k}, and νk−1\nu_{k-1}, while QkIQ_{k}^{I} and αk\alpha_{k} are hidden. Before entering either network, SS is centred at 100, YY is multiplied by 1,000, and ξ\xi and the previous action are divided by 100; we found these rescaling provides better results as they place the network inputs on comparable numerical scales; the dynamics and reported payoffs remain in the model’s original units.

After the action has been executed, the broker observes Qk+1BQ_{k+1}^{B} and can reconstruct the informed flow from the inventory transition:

(7) ηk=νk−ξk−Qk+1B−QkBΔ​t.\eta_{k}=\nu_{k}-\xi_{k}-\frac{Q_{k+1}^{B}-Q_{k}^{B}}{\Delta t}.

The broker therefore cannot use ηk\eta_{k} when choosing νk\nu_{k}, but can use the reconstructed value when forming its estimates for decision k+1k+1.

The analytical payoff is undiscounted, so we set γRL=1\gamma_{\mathrm{RL}}=1.

3.4. Environment Step

We use PPO as our main algorithm (Schulman et al., 2017) and compare FFNN and LSTM actors, each trained for four million environment transitions. At time tkt_{k}, the policy samples a raw action νkπ\nu_{k}^{\pi} (“Raw” denotes the network output before clipping), while the environment executes νk=clip⁡(νkπ,−100,100)\nu_{k}=\operatorname{clip}(\nu_{k}^{\pi},-100,100), as shown in Figure 1. PPO evaluates the likelihood of the raw action during training. We record how often clipping occurs and the size of the adjustment between the raw and executed actions. The informed trader calculates ηk⋆\eta_{k}^{\star} from the state at time kk before either action changes the state.

4. Experimental Results

We now answer the research questions introduced in Section 1. Block A verifies the reference action νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}} used throughout the experiments. Blocks B–C answer RQ1 by testing full-information PPO, actor capacity under supervised learning, the PPO critic’s ability to rank nearby actions, and potential-based reward shaping. Block D answers RQ2 by comparing partial-information PPO with a certainty-equivalent (CE) controller. Section 5 answers RQ3.

Table 1 gives the training settings; code and fixed experiment configurations will be released after peer review. Each PPO configuration uses five training seeds and four million transitions per seed. Because PPO performance can deteriorate late in training, we evaluate checkpoints every 0.4 million transitions on 50 validation paths and select the checkpoint with the highest average broker payoff. After checkpoint selection, every trained policy is evaluated on the same 250 test paths, which are not used for training or checkpoint selection. The reported 95% Student-tt intervals are calculated across five independently trained policies, all evaluated on the same test paths.

4.1. Block A: Continuous and finite-grid alignment

Block A tests whether the comparison with PPO is affected by discretising the continuous-time game. The simulator applies Equation (2) at every step of the Euler–Maruyama simulator. Let xk=(QkB,QkI,Yk,αk,ξk)𝖳x_{k}=(Q_{k}^{B},Q_{k}^{I},Y_{k},\alpha_{k},\xi_{k})^{\mathsf{T}}. The finite-grid linear–quadratic (LQ) action is Kk​xkK_{k}x_{k}, where KkK_{k} is the time-dependent feedback vector obtained from the backward recursion below. We use the reference action as shown in Figure 1, νkref=clip⁡(Kk​xk,−100,100).\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}}=\operatorname{clip}(K_{k}x_{k},-100,100). This gives a feasible reference in the PPO action range; the unconstrained LQ action is Kk​xkK_{k}x_{k}.

To solve the finite-grid problem, write the Euler transition and reward as

4.2. Block B: Full-information PPO recovery

We first set ξ=0\xi=0, the zero-uninformed-flow model also considered in (Cartea et al., 2026). We then set σξ=100\sigma_{\xi}=100 to introduce stochastic uninformed flow. Five independently initialised policies per architecture observe the full state and train for four million transitions. We compare each action by the policy with νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}}.

For the zero-flow FFNN, we use an initial log standard deviation of 33. Table 2(b) reports an LQ loss of 0.045±0.0310.045\mathbin{\pm}0.031 and an action RMSE of 5.494±2.1635.494\mathbin{\pm}2.163 across five independently trained roots. Figure 2 shows that the selected FFNN approaches the zero-flow reference, whereas the LSTM remains inaccurate. Table 2(d) shows that the PPO agents tested with σξ=100\sigma_{\xi}=100 also remain inaccurate. Thus, for RQ1, PPO–FFNN can approach the full-information strategy when ξ=0\xi=0, but we do not obtain similar performance after introducing stochastic uninformed flow.

4.3. Block C: Actor capacity and learning diagnostics

Block C tests whether the FFNN and LSTM can reproduce νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}} when that action is supplied directly. With ξ=0\xi=0, we train a ReLU FFNN and a Tanh LSTM through supervised learning, using νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}} as labels and the supervised learning has the same architectures as the PPO actors. We evaluate them on analytical test trajectories and then allow each actor to control the simulator.

Table 2(c) shows that supervised learning substantially reduces the test error of both architectures. The supervised FFNN also remains close to the reference when it controls the simulator, whereas the LSTM result varies considerably across training seeds. Supervised learning therefore shows that both networks can approximate νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}} during testing. Figure 2 shows the performance of the models.

Reward and critic diagnostics:

Starting from the full-information baseline (σξ=100\sigma_{\xi}=100, ReLU FFNN), we change one component at a time to probe the sensitivity of PPO. The analytical broker action and corrected reward do not depend on the midprice SkS_{k}. We therefore remove SkS_{k} to test whether this input makes PPO learning more difficult, and varify the effects of the Δ​t2\Delta t^{2} correction by removing it or multiplying the reward by 100. Every condition uses five seeds, four million training transitions per seed, and the same numbers of validation and test paths. Table 3 reports the resulting payoff, action RMSE, and critic explained variance. Removing the Δ​t2\Delta t^{2} correction or the price input SkS_{k} does not produce a consistent payoff change across seeds. Multiplying the reward by 100 lowers the payoff for every seed, showing that PPO is sensitive to reward scale.

PPO learns a state-value function Vθ​(s)V_{\theta}(s). Since γRL=1\gamma_{\mathrm{RL}}=1, the Bellman relation gives

Qkπ(s,a)=𝔼[rk(s,a)+Vk+1π(sk+1)∣sk=s,νk=a].Q_{k}^{\pi}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[r_{k}(s,a)+V_{k+1}^{\pi}(s_{k+1})\mid s_{k}=s,\nu_{k}=a\right].

We test whether the critic correctly ranks two actions near the trained policy. At a test state ss that is not used to train or select the critic, let ν¯π​(s)\bar{\nu}_{\pi}(s) be the deterministic policy action and set a±=clip⁡(ν¯π​(s)±10,−100,100)a_{\pm}=\operatorname{clip}(\bar{\nu}_{\pi}(s)\pm 10,-100,100). Clipping is inactive in these 120 comparisons, so the two actions are 20 units apart. For Monte Carlo sample ℓ\ell, rkℓ​(s,a)r_{k}^{\ell}(s,a) is the immediate reward after taking action aa, and sk+1(a,ℓ)s_{k+1}^{(a,\ell)} is the resulting next state. Replacing VπV^{\pi} with VθV_{\theta} and averaging over LL simulated transitions gives

Δ​Q^θ,k\displaystyle\Delta\widehat{Q}_{\theta,k} =1L​∑ℓ=1L[(rkℓ​(s,a+)+Vθ​(sk+1(a+,ℓ)))⏟Q^θ,kℓ​(s,a+)−(rkℓ​(s,a−)+Vθ​(sk+1(a−,ℓ)))⏟Q^θ,kℓ​(s,a−)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\Biggl[\underbrace{\Bigl(r_{k}^{\ell}(s,a_{+})+V_{\theta}(s_{k+1}^{(a_{+},\ell)})\Bigr)}_{\widehat{Q}_{\theta,k}^{\ell}(s,a_{+})}-\underbrace{\Bigl(r_{k}^{\ell}(s,a_{-})+V_{\theta}(s_{k+1}^{(a_{-},\ell)})\Bigr)}_{\widehat{Q}_{\theta,k}^{\ell}(s,a_{-})}\Biggr],
(17) Δ​QkMC\displaystyle\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathrm{MC}} =1L​∑ℓ=1L[𝒢k,ℓπ​(a+)−𝒢k,ℓπ​(a−)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\bigl[\mathcal{G}_{k,\ell}^{\pi}(a_{+})-\mathcal{G}_{k,\ell}^{\pi}(a_{-})\bigr],

where 𝒢k,ℓπ​(a)=rkℓ​(s,a)+∑j=k+1N−1rjℓ​(sja,ℓ,νjπ),\mathcal{G}_{k,\ell}^{\pi}(a)=r_{k}^{\ell}(s,a)+\sum_{j=k+1}^{N-1}r_{j}^{\ell}\left(s_{j}^{a,\ell},\nu_{j}^{\pi}\right), is the sum of the remaining rewards from Monte Carlo sampling after selecting action aa at decision kk. Δ​Q^θ,k\Delta\widehat{Q}_{\theta,k} is the action preference predicted by the critic using the immediate reward and next-state value, while Δ​QkMC\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathrm{MC}} is the action preference estimated from the complete simulated returns (if Δ​Q^θ,k\Delta\widehat{Q}_{\theta,k} and Δ​QkMC\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathrm{MC}} have the same sign, it indicates that the critic correctly ranks the two actions). The two candidate actions use the same market innovations and future policy noise, and L=32L=32 Monte Carlo simulations are averaged for each comparison.

We also compare Vθ​(s)V_{\theta}(s) with the Monte Carlo return of the current policy at 24 test states per seed. The critics can distinguish states with generally higher or lower expected remaining returns, but Figure 3 shows that they cannot reliably rank two nearby actions taken from the same state. Inaccurate local action ranking is therefore a plausible source of weak PPO performance in ξ=100\xi=100.

Potential-based reward shaping:

We next test whether the long-horizon broker payoff provides insufficient information about the quality of each action. The potential Vk⋆​(x)=x𝖳​Fk​x+ckV_{k}^{\star}(x)=x^{\mathsf{T}}F_{k}x+c_{k} is computed from the finite-grid LQ solution, which is used to shape our reward from Equation (12). The PPO is trained with

rkshape\displaystyle r_{k}^{\mathrm{shape}} =rk+Vk+1⋆​(xk+1)−Vk⋆​(xk),\displaystyle=r_{k}+V_{k+1}^{\star}(x_{k+1})-V_{k}^{\star}(x_{k}),
(18) 𝔼[rkshape∣xk,νk]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r_{k}^{\mathrm{shape}}\mid x_{k},\nu_{k}] =χk​(νk−Kk​xk)2≤0.\displaystyle=\chi_{k}\bigl(\nu_{k}-K_{k}x_{k}\bigr)^{2}\leq 0.

Because VN⋆=0V_{N}^{\star}=0 and the initial state is fixed, the shaped and original episode returns differ by the same constant. Reward shaping therefore changes the learning signal without changing the ordering of policies (Ng et al., 1999). Since Kk​xkK_{k}x_{k} is calculated from the unconstrained finite-grid LQ problem it can produce trading speeds that lie outside the action range, the squared term measures deviation from the unconstrained LQ action.

We train ten FFNN policies, five with the original reward in Equation (12) and 5 with the shaped reward in Equation (18). Each pair has the same initial weights, market paths, and training settings. Shaping increases mean payoff by 1.571.57 (95% interval [-5.00,8.14]) and reduces action RMSE by 1.761.76 (95% interval [-4.50,8.02]); both changes are favourable in three of five seeds. It also increases the per-step reward standard deviation by approximately 75%. Raw training actions cross the feasible range in approximately 0.1% of decisions under either reward. Under this protocol, shaping changes the learning signal but does not reliably recover νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}}.

4.4. Block D: Partial-information control

Block D asks how closely PPO can approach the causal CE controller when both use the same information available before each decision. PPO observes (S,QB,Y,ξ,τ,νk−1)(S,Q^{B},Y,\xi,\tau,\nu_{k-1}), while QIQ^{I}, α\alpha, and the current informed-trader rate are hidden before acting. The CE controller uses the game dynamics and the broker’s causal history

ℋkB=σ⁡(o0P,ν0,…,νk−1,okP)\mathcal{H}_{k}^{B}=\sigma(o_{0}^{P},\nu_{0},\ldots,\nu_{k-1},o_{k}^{P})

to estimate the hidden components QkIQ_{k}^{I} and αk\alpha_{k}. It then substitutes these estimates into the finite-grid feedback rule:

νkCE=Π𝒜​(Kk​x^k).\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{CE}}=\Pi_{\mathcal{A}}\!\left(K_{k}\widehat{x}_{k}\right).

Specifically, the CE controller forms

Q^k|k−I=𝔼⁡[QkI∣ℋkB],α^k|k−=𝔼⁡[αk∣ℋkB].\widehat{Q}^{I}_{k\mid k^{-}}=\mathbb{E}[Q_{k}^{I}\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}^{B}],\qquad\widehat{\alpha}_{k\mid k^{-}}=\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{k}\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}^{B}].

After observing Qk+1BQ_{k+1}^{B}, the controller reconstructs the informed flow that has already occurred and updates the informed trader’s inventory:

(19) ηkrec\displaystyle\eta_{k}^{\mathrm{rec}} =νk−ξk−Qk+1B−QkBΔ​t,\displaystyle=\nu_{k}-\xi_{k}-\frac{Q_{k+1}^{B}-Q_{k}^{B}}{\Delta t},
Q^k+1|k+1−I\displaystyle\widehat{Q}^{I}_{k+1\mid k+1^{-}} =Q^k|k−I+ηkrec​Δ​t.\displaystyle=\widehat{Q}^{I}_{k\mid k^{-}}+\eta_{k}^{\mathrm{rec}}\Delta t.

Writing Pi​j,k=Pi​j​(tk)P_{ij,k}=P_{ij}(t_{k}) and hi,k=hi​(tk)h_{i,k}=h_{i}(t_{k}), we rearrange the informed trader’s feedback equation to estimate the signal:

(20) α^k|k\displaystyle\widehat{\alpha}_{k\mid k} =(ηkrec−P21,k​QkB−P22,k​Q^k|k−ICLOSE\displaystyle=\bigl(\eta_{k}^{\mathrm{rec}}-P_{21,k}Q_{k}^{B}-P_{22,k}\widehat{Q}^{I}_{k\mid k^{-}}
OPEN−P23,k​Yk−h2,k​ξk)/h1,k,\displaystyle-P_{23,k}Y_{k}-h_{2,k}\xi_{k}\bigr)/h_{1,k},
α^k+1|(k+1)−\displaystyle\widehat{\alpha}_{k+1\mid(k+1)^{-}} =ρα​α^k|k.\displaystyle=\rho_{\alpha}\widehat{\alpha}_{k\mid k}.

The estimated informed-trader inventory and predictive signal are combined with the observed state variables to calculate the CE action νk+1CE\nu_{k+1}^{\mathrm{CE}} at the next decision. On 250 test paths, the reconstructed informed-trader inventory has negligible error, while the predicted signal and pre-action informed flow have RMSE 0.0141 and 0.873. The remaining error is caused by the new signal innovation, which is unavailable before the broker acts.

Table 2(d) shows that the CE controller remains close to νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}}, while both partial-information PPO agents have substantially lower payoffs and larger action errors. The broker’s observable history therefore contains enough information for accurate control in this environment, but the PPO agents do not learn to use that history as effectively. This answers RQ2.

5. Adapting the Analytical Policy with PPO

We now address RQ3 by testing the direction we introduced in Section 1 and proposed in (Ning et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026): using an analytical policy as the starting point for RL. Our propsed method would be to freeze the analytical broker action and train PPO to correct execution-cost misspecification through a residual adjustment (Johannink et al., 2019).

Let ℰ⁡(a)\mathcal{E}(a) denote the broker environment with execution-cost coefficient aa. We calculate the analytical policy in the original environment ℰ0=ℰ⁡(a0)\mathcal{E}_{0}=\mathcal{E}(a_{0}), where a0=0.0012a_{0}=0.0012, and train the PPO adjustment in ℰnew=ℰ⁡(atrue)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{new}}=\mathcal{E}(a_{\mathrm{true}}).

Frozen analytical policy:

In ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0}, we evaluate and store the analytical coefficients P11,P12,P13P_{11},P_{12},P_{13} and g1,g2g_{1},g_{2} from (Cartea et al., 2026), with the optimal action

(21) νkℰ0=P110​(tk)​QkB+P120​(tk)​QkI+P130​(tk)​Yk+g10​(tk)​αk+g20​(tk)​ξk.\nu_{k}^{\mathcal{E}_{0}}=P_{11}^{0}(t_{k})Q_{k}^{B}+P_{12}^{0}(t_{k})Q_{k}^{I}+P_{13}^{0}(t_{k})Y_{k}+g_{1}^{0}(t_{k})\alpha_{k}+g_{2}^{0}(t_{k})\xi_{k}.

Equation (21) has the same broker-feedback form as Equation (2), and the superscript 00 identifies coefficients calculated in ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0}. On 100 test paths generated at a0a_{0}, the frozen and replayed analytical trajectories have trading-speed and inventory RMSEs of 6.36×10−76.36\times 10^{-7} and 3.29×10−93.29\times 10^{-9}, respectively.

PPO adjustment after a cost change:

In ℰnew=ℰ⁡(atrue)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{new}}=\mathcal{E}(a_{\mathrm{true}}), the analytical action calculated in ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} remains fixed and PPO learns an additive correction:

(22) μ⁡(ok)=νkℰ0+δ​ν​(ok).\mu(o_{k})=\nu_{k}^{\mathcal{E}_{0}}+\delta\nu(o_{k}).

Here, νkℰ0\nu_{k}^{\mathcal{E}_{0}} is the action generated by the frozen analytical policy and δ​ν​(ok)\delta\nu(o_{k}) is the residual adjustment learned by PPO. The residual is a two-layer, width-64 Tanh FFNN of the full-information observation in ℰnew\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{new}} (we also tested the ReLU setup from Block B, the wider exploration improves learning when ξ=0\xi=0, but it lowers payoff for all five residual policies; thus we found this Tanh setup to be the best for our misspecification problem). Its output layer is initialised at zero, so the initial policy mean equals νkℰ0\nu_{k}^{\mathcal{E}_{0}}. PPO then trains the residual without an additional adjustment bound or penalty. Gaussian exploration is centred on the combined mean, and the environment clips sampled actions to [−100,100][-100,100]. Table 1 reports the remaining training settings.

All three cost experiments use full information and σξ=100\sigma_{\xi}=100. We test atrue∈{0.0006,0.0012,0.0018}a_{\mathrm{true}}\in\{0.0006,0.0012,0.0018\} in ℰnew\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{new}}. The informed trader’s coefficients are recomputed at the true cost, while the broker retains the coefficients from ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} and does not observe atruea_{\mathrm{true}} as an input. A separate PPO adjustment is trained for each cost. For evaluation, νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}} is recomputed at the true cost. For each seed, we evaluate five checkpoints on 50 validation paths and, as in Section 4, select the checkpoint with the highest mean finite-grid broker payoff. The selected policy is then evaluated on 100 common test paths.

When the execution cost is halved, all five PPO adjustments improve the test payoff. The mean increase is 0.005190.00519, with a 95% interval of [0.00296,0.00743][0.00296,0.00743] across the five independently trained policies, and closes 2.22%2.22\% of the gap between the unchanged policy and the changed-cost reference. The largest residual action on the lower-cost test paths is 1.41, and final-action clipping occurs on 0.029% of decisions. PPO therefore provides a small, repeatable improvement only in the lower-cost case tested here.

6. Discussion and Conclusion

We studied whether PPO can recover and subsequently adapt an analytically known broker strategy. For RQ1, we have shown that PPO–FFNN approaches νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}} under full information when ξ=0\xi=0, however when ξ=100\xi=100, the policies remain inaccurate. The finite-step reward and grid-refinement results show that these errors are not caused by numerical issues, while supervised learning shows that the FFNN can approximate and execute the reference action on states generated by the analytical policy. The critic diagnostic shows inaccurate local action ranking can contribute to the difficulty of learning from rewards.

For RQ2, the certainty-equivalent controller remains close to the reference action νkref\nu_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}} when the informed trader’s inventory and signal are hidden. Its performance shows that the available history supports accurate control in this environment, while PPO–FFNN and PPO–LSTM do not learn to use that information as effectively.

For RQ3, the frozen analytical policy provides an accurate starting strategy after the execution cost changes. Residual PPO produces a small and repeatable payoff improvement when the cost is halved. The analytical solution is therefore useful both as a benchmark for diagnosing learned policies and as a prior for subsequent adaptation, thus providing some evidence of analytical policy initialisation being useful (Ning et al., 2021).

The numerical checks and supervised learning make discretisation, reward implementation, and insufficient FFNN capacity unlikely to be the primary limitations. A more plausible explanation is the interaction between exploration and reward-based value estimation. Wider initial exploration improves PPO when ξ=0\xi=0, but performance remains poor after stochastic uninformed flow is introduced, where the critic also shows weak local action ranking. Partial information additionally requires relevant information to be recovered from past observations. When an analytical policy is already available, wider exploration can instead move the adjustment away from a useful starting point, while conservative adjustments produce a small improvement under the lower-cost misspecification.

Future work can use analytical value or action-value information to improve the local learning signal, study alternative action and policy parameterisations, and develop structured residual policies for nonlinear costs or uncertain market impact. Under partial information, it would be interesting to test the performance of the model by introducing a filter into the actor, and practical applications for the partial information setting would include having a ξ+η\xi+\eta flow.
